notes.gyendi: The usual reply to Habari? Even on a bad day, people answer Nzuri first.
notes.karibu: Also the answer to Asante: “you’re welcome”.
notes.jambo: Friendly and simple; you’ll hear it most with visitors. Among friends, people say Mambo? or Habari?
notes.shikamoo: Said to an elder. Only the elder says it back: Marahaba.
notes.weraba: To one person. To several people: Kwaherini.
notes.lyange: Agrees with jina: jina langu, my name.
notes.lyo: Agrees with jina: jina lako, your name.
notes.ani: Jina lako nani? asks “your name is who?”
notes.ni: “Is/am/are” for every person: Mimi ni mwanafunzi, I am a student.
notes.bulungi: For many ki- things (vikombe vizuri), and on its own: “well”.

guidebook.intro: Nobody in East Africa gets straight to business. You greet first, ask how things are, and only then ask for directions or the price of mangoes.

tips.title: Every greeting asks for news
body: **Habari** means “news”, so **Habari?** is “any news?”. Add the time of day: **Habari za asubuhi?** (news of the morning?), **Habari za mchana?** (news of the afternoon?).
The polite answer is always good news first: **Nzuri**, **Salama** (peaceful) or **Njema** (good). If something is wrong, you say so after.

tips.title: Ni: one little word for am, is and are
body: **Ni** links two things for every person: **Mimi ni Emma** (I am Emma), **Wewe ni nani?** (who are you?), **Jina langu ni Amani** (my name is Amani).
“My” and “your” come after the noun and agree with it: **jina langu**, **jina lako**. You’ll see them change with other nouns in the next unit.

tips.title: Say it as it’s written
body: Swahili spelling is regular: every letter is pronounced, and the vowels **a e i o u** sound like in Spanish or Italian. The stress almost always falls on the second-to-last syllable: a-SAN-te, ka-RI-bu, kwa-HE-ri.

culture.title: Shikamoo for elders
body: In Tanzania especially, young people greet anyone clearly older with **Shikamoo**, and the elder answers **Marahaba**. It is never said to someone younger, and saying it to a friend your own age is a joke.

culture.title: Karibu means you are expected
body: You will hear **Karibu** everywhere: at a door, in a shop, after “thank you”. A guest is usually offered a seat and something to drink before anything else is said.
